# Lease Clause Checker: full details

The [short version](../README.md) is on the front page. This page has the method, every result table, the tools and the limitations.

An evaluation of large language models on Ontario residential lease clauses: can they tell which
terms the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 makes void, and does giving a light model the Act's
text, with every quote it gives checked in code, let it answer as well as a heavy one?

<!-- tldr:start (generated by `make report`; edit scoreboard.py, not this) -->
**TL;DR**

- Closed book (no statute text in the prompt), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 3.8 Flash got all 38 verdicts right, yet 13 and 19 of their 38 quotes, respectively, failed the word-for-word check (4 and 8 of them differing only cosmetically or by quoting conventions). With the statute in the prompt, 150 of 151 first pipeline answers with a verdict on the main set, from the 4 models, had a quote that passed.
- Every pipeline verdict comes with a citation a reader can check: a section of the Act and a quote from it that code has checked word for word (`lcc check` adds a link to the section on e-Laws). If the quote fails twice, the answer is `unsure`, not an unchecked citation. Of 208 pipeline answers (4 models, 52 clauses), 207 had a checked quote; 1 was the model's own `unsure`. A checked quote shows the words are in the Act, not that the section decides the clause: 4 of the 207 cited a section the label doesn't accept.
- On the 38-clause main set (synthetic clauses; the pipeline is given the text of the rule sections), Claude Haiku 5.5 with the pipeline got 38 of 38 verdicts right for $0.036; Claude Opus 5.5 alone got 38 of 38 for $0.77. 38 clauses can't tell them apart.
- For Claude Haiku 5.5, the statute text moved the verdicts, not the quote check: closed book, it got 21 of 38 verdicts right; with the text, 38. The check failed 1 of 207 checked first answers (c14: Claude Haiku 5.5 dropped words from the middle of s. 27(2)), and the retry changed no verdict.
- A right section is not a right answer: on c01, Claude Haiku 5.5's baseline cited s. 14, which voids no-pet provisions, and still called the clause enforceable.
- Cost followed each model's default thinking setting, not its tier: Gemini 3.8 Flash with the pipeline cost $0.68 on the main set, 79% of it for thinking tokens, and Gemini 4 Argon alone $0.072. By the same method, too, Gemini 3.8 Flash cost more (baseline $0.18 vs $0.072; pipeline $0.68 vs $0.40); at its default, Gemini 4 Argon did not think on any baseline answer.
<!-- tldr:end -->

> **Not legal advice.** This is a research and evaluation project. Its output may be wrong. If
> you have a question about your tenancy, contact a lawyer, a community legal clinic, or the
> Landlord and Tenant Board.

## Why

A chatbot answer can sound right and still cite the wrong section of the law, or no section at
all. A reader has no easy way to tell. This project measures how often that happens and tests one
mitigation.

## Approach

1. Give the model the relevant sections of the
   [Residential Tenancies Act, 2006](https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17) (Ontario).
2. Require structured output: a verdict (`void` / `allowed` / `unsure`), a section number, and a
   verbatim quote from that section.
3. Check in code that the quote really appears in the cited section, after normalising
   whitespace and quotation marks.
4. Retry once if the check fails; otherwise return `unsure`.

The same synthetic test clauses are run through a plain "is this enforceable?" prompt as a
baseline, and both methods are scored with deterministic code (no LLM judge) on verdict accuracy,
false alarms on lawful clauses, citation validity, and how often the model says `unsure`.

## Status

Work in progress. These exist:

- the statute fetcher;
- the rule list ([data/rules.yaml](../data/rules.yaml)): 18 RTA sections, each with its e-Laws
  heading, a one-line paraphrase and a link;
- a test set of 38 synthetic clauses ([data/clauses.jsonl](../data/clauses.jsonl)), covering 16
  of the 18 rules, frozen before any model saw it (see [data/README.md](../data/README.md)).
  The author reviewed every label by hand, with LLM assistance (main set 11 Nov, stress set
  13 Nov). No lawyer has reviewed them.
  s. 4 decides no clause on its own, and s. 22 turns on facts about how much interference
  there was.

- a baseline: the plain prompt in [prompts/baseline-v1.txt](../prompts/baseline-v1.txt), run on a
  light and a heavy model from Anthropic and from Google, paired by tier: Claude Haiku 5.5 with
  Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5 with Gemini 4 Argon
  ([models.py](../src/lease_clause_checker/models.py) records the model ids and prices). Every raw
  answer is saved in [results/](../results/) with the model, prompt version and date, and scoring
  is deterministic code that reads only the answer's final "Verdict:" and "Section:" lines.

- the grounded pipeline ([pipeline.py](../src/lease_clause_checker/pipeline.py), prompt in
  [prompts/pipeline-v1.txt](../prompts/pipeline-v1.txt)): the text of all 18 rule sections in
  the prompt, a JSON answer (verdict `void` / `allowed` / `unsure`, section, quote, reason),
  a quote check in code ([verify.py](../src/lease_clause_checker/verify.py)), one retry that tells
  the model what failed, and `unsure` if the retry fails too. A quote passes when, after
  whitespace and quotation marks are normalised, it appears word for word within one
  subsection of the cited section and has at least five words, not counting markers such as
  "(2)" or "(a)". Quoting a heading is reported separately from a quote that isn't there.

- a closed-book run ([closedbook.py](../src/lease_clause_checker/closedbook.py), prompt in
  [prompts/closedbook-v1.txt](../prompts/closedbook-v1.txt)): the pipeline's question and JSON
  answer with no statute text, asked once with no retry, the quote checked by the same code.
  It measures whether a model recalls the Act's words, and is reported apart
  ([Closed book](#closed-book-the-pipelines-question-without-the-statute)).

- a stress set of 14 clauses chosen because Claude Haiku 5.5 got them wrong
  ([data/README.md](../data/README.md#stressjsonl-the-stress-set)), reported apart from the main
  set.

- a demo command, `lcc check`, that runs the pipeline on each clause of a lease
  ([check.py](../src/lease_clause_checker/check.py); see [Check a lease](#check-a-lease)), and
  `lcc quote check`, the quote check on its own (see [Check a quote](#check-a-quote)).

- an MCP server, `lcc mcp`, that gives a model the Act's sections and checks its quotes, one
  at a time or every quote and citation in a draft
  ([mcp_server.py](../src/lease_clause_checker/mcp_server.py); see
  [Use the quote check from Claude](#use-the-quote-check-from-claude-mcp)).

- a static explorer of the four models' saved answers and the hand check, `lcc site`
  ([explorer.py](../src/lease_clause_checker/explorer.py); see
  [Explore the saved answers](#explore-the-saved-answers)).

Results are in [Results](#results) below.

To re-score everything and regenerate the results below, offline:

```sh
uv sync
uv run lcc statute fetch      # the Act, needed for the pipeline and for scoring citations
make report                   # rewrites the Results section and results/scoreboard.svg
```

To re-run a method (`run` calls paid APIs; answers already in `results/` are reused) or see
every wrong answer: `uv run lcc baseline run`, `uv run lcc pipeline report --details`,
`uv run lcc closedbook report --details`, and so on. Add `--clauses data/stress.jsonl` for the stress set.

None of the four models accepts a temperature setting, so each runs with its provider's
default sampling; reproducibility comes from the saved answers, not from re-calling the APIs.

### Check a lease

```sh
cp .env.example .env                        # then add ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
uv run lcc statute fetch
uv run lcc check samples/lease_short.txt
```

[samples/lease_short.txt](../samples/lease_short.txt) is a short synthetic lease written for the
demo. Its clauses are not copied from the test set, but most of them test the same rules as
test-set clauses (clause 3 and c25, for example), so the demo is not an out-of-sample result.
Each numbered clause gets the pipeline's verdict, the section it cites, the quote (checked
against the Act's text) and a link to the section on e-Laws. The model is Claude Haiku 5.5
unless `--model` names another. Each clause costs one paid call, or two when a quote fails the
check; the answers are saved, so checking the same lease again costs nothing. The sample's
answers are committed in [results/check/](../results/check/), so the command above replays them
without a key. Only the 18 rule sections are in the prompt, so a clause about anything else
may get a wrong or `unsure` answer. Two of the eight clauses, from a run on 14 November 2026
(UTC):

```text
  2  VOID     Pets are not allowed in the apartment or the building.
              s. 14, “No pet” provisions void
              “A provision in a tenancy agreement prohibiting the presence of
              animals in or about the residential complex is void.”
              https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17#BK19

  6  VOID     This lease ends automatically when the one-year term is over, and
              the Tenant must leave the unit on that day.
              s. 37, Termination only in accordance with Act
              “A tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with this Act.”
              https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17#BK47
```

### Check a quote

`lcc quote check` runs the pipeline's quote check on one quote, offline, against the cached
Act. It exits 0 if the quote verifies and 1 if it doesn't, and says where a failed quote first
leaves the Act's wording, and which words of the quote's sentence in the Act it leaves out
before and after it. Changing one word of the s. 14 quote above:

```text
$ uv run lcc quote check 14 "A provision in a tenancy agreement prohibiting the presence of dogs in or about the residential complex is void."
NOT VERIFIED: The quote does not appear word for word in section 14.
The first 10 words match s. 14; then the quote has “dogs” where the Act has “animals”.
Source: Ontario e-Laws. Not an official version of the statute. © King's Printer for Ontario, 2006.
Not legal advice: this checks the wording only, not what it means.
```

Claude Opus 5.5's closed-book quote for clause c05 fails at "tenancy,"; it also leaves out the
words of s. 15 that make such a provision void. The left-out words are the rest of the quote's
sentence in the Act before and after the words it matches (for a quote in a list item, the
list's lead-in and the rest of its own item). They are a report: they change neither the check
nor the quote's category.

```text
$ uv run lcc quote check 15 "all or part of the remaining rent for a term or tenancy, or a specific sum, becomes due and payable if the tenant defaults in the payment of rent due"
NOT VERIFIED: The quote does not appear word for word in section 15.
The first 11 words match s. 15; then the quote has “tenancy,” where the Act has “period”.
Words of its sentence in s. 15 that it leaves out: before it, “A provision in a
tenancy agreement providing that”; after it, “or in carrying out an obligation
is void”.
Source: Ontario e-Laws. Not an official version of the statute. © King's Printer for Ontario, 2006.
Not legal advice: this checks the wording only, not what it means.
```

A quote that passes can still stop before the words that decide the clause. It still exits 0,
with a warning (from `verify.ending`, a rough rule) and the Act's next words:

```text
$ uv run lcc quote check 108 "Neither a landlord nor a tenancy agreement shall require a tenant or prospective tenant to,"
VERIFIED: the quote appears word for word in s. 108.
Warning: word for word, but it may stop before the words that decide it. The Act
goes on: “(a) provide post-dated cheques or other negotiable instruments for
payment of rent; or (b) permit automatic debiting of the tenant's …”
Source: Ontario e-Laws. Not an official version of the statute. © King's Printer for Ontario, 2006.
Not legal advice: this checks the wording only, not what it means.
```

### Use the quote check from Claude (MCP)

`lcc mcp` runs an MCP server over stdio with three read-only tools on the cached e-Laws copy
of the Act (not an official version):

- `get_section(act, section)`: a section's in-force text, with its heading, e-Laws link,
  consolidation period, retrieval date and the King's Printer notice. A subsection in the
  citation ("s. 27(2)") is also returned on its own (a paragraph such as "(a)" is not).
- `verify_quote(act, section, quote)`: the strict check and the check with quoting
  conventions, the quote's category (verbatim, drops a negation, passes with quoting
  conventions, cosmetic, wrong section cited, content words differ, not in the Act), a one-line
  summary and a word-level diff against the Act. The whole cited section is searched; the
  summary says if the quote is in another subsection than the one cited. A verbatim quote that
  may stop before the words that decide it gets a warning with the Act's next words, and the
  words of the quote's sentence that it leaves out before or after it are named; neither
  changes the strict check or the category.
- `check_text(text)`: every quote (in double quotation marks) and section citation in a
  draft, such as a memo. Each quote is checked as `verify_quote` checks it, against the
  citation right after it in its sentence (`"… is void" (s. 14)`), else the nearest one before
  it in the sentence. A quote with no citation is checked against the section whose wording is
  closest, and a citation with no quote is reported as in force or not. Citations of another
  statute ("s. 67 of the Legislation Act, 2006") are listed and not checked, and so is a
  quotation mark with no partner in its paragraph. The rules are in
  [drafts.py](../src/lease_clause_checker/drafts.py). It reports wording only and gives no
  verdict on any clause.

`act` is `"RTA"`; the server has only the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. The tools read the
cache under the repository's `.cache/` and call no network or model. They check wording, not
legal meaning, and are not legal advice.

First, in the repository: `uv sync` and `uv run lcc statute fetch`. Then, to add the server to
Claude Code for every project (`--scope user`; leave it out to add it to the current project
only):

```sh
claude mcp add --scope user lease-clause-checker -- uv --directory /path/to/lease-clause-checker run lcc mcp
```

For Claude Desktop, add this to `claude_desktop_config.json` and restart it. Desktop apps may
not see your shell's `PATH`, so give the full path to `uv` (from `which uv`):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "lease-clause-checker": {
      "command": "/full/path/to/uv",
      "args": ["--directory", "/path/to/lease-clause-checker", "run", "lcc", "mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

### Explore the saved answers

The explorer is a static page that replays the saved answers; it calls no model. It is
published at <https://present42.github.io/lease-clause-checker/>: the `gh-pages` branch holds
the `lcc site` export of a commit on `main` (with a `.nojekyll` file), and a new export pushed
there replaces it at the same address. To view it locally:

```sh
uv run lcc site                                  # writes site/ (gitignored)
python3 -m http.server 8000 --directory site     # then open http://localhost:8000
```

It opens on three closed-book answers with a right verdict and a quote that, by the hand check,
changes what the Act says and would mislead on the clause: Claude Opus 5.5 on c26, Gemini
3.8 Flash on c09 and Claude Haiku 5.5 on c15, named with a label and a punchline in
[exhibits.yaml](../src/lease_clause_checker/exhibits.yaml). `make report` and `lcc site` refuse
an exhibit unless its verdict is right, its hand check says yes to both questions, and its
punchline starts by stating the verdict; the README leads with the first. Each shows the clause
and the verdict, the Act's subsection, and below it a box that starts as a copy of the
subsection and replays the model's edits one at a time, in reading order: the dropped words
strike through and fold away (and are marked in the Act's box), the added words type in. The
edits come from the same alignment as the redline (`exhibits.replay`, from `Alignment.runs`),
and the export stops unless they end at the saved quote, token for token. Each replay plays
once when it comes into view, one at a time; Replay plays it again, and Next change, or the right arrow key,
steps one edit at a time (the left arrow steps back). With reduced motion the page shows the
finished state. Under each exhibit, "The model's reason" (closed at first) gives the answer's
own reason, word for word, and an optional one-line note from the configuration says more about
the exhibit. Above them, the opening screen gives the base rate (how many right closed-book
verdicts came with a quote that would mislead) and what "would mislead" means. Then come the
four-model table and the hand check's counts. Its other views:
- **Misquotes**: the closed-book answers with a right verdict whose quote is not word for word,
  by model;
- **Grid**: every closed-book verdict and quote check;
- **By clause**: every answer to each clause, by method and model, for the main test set and the
  hard cases (the stress set);
- **Hand check**: the closed-book quotes that failed, with how the check was made; the ones that
  would mislead are highlighted.

Every quote is shown as one redline against the whole subsection it lines up with, the same one
the README shows (`Alignment.pieces(whole=True)`): the Act's words that the quote leaves out or
replaces struck through in red, including those before and after it, and the quote's own words
underlined in blue. A one-line bar under the header gives the caveats (not legal advice; checks
wording, not legal meaning; word for word is not complete; not an official version), and the
opening view and the foot of every other page give them in full. Its fonts (Source Serif 4,
IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono, under the SIL Open Font License) are served with it from
`explorer_assets/fonts/`, so the page asks no other site for anything and works offline;
[fonts/README.md](../src/lease_clause_checker/explorer_assets/fonts/README.md) says where each
file comes from.

The preview image for links to the page, `explorer_assets/og.png`, is the page's `#/card` view:
the first exhibit's redline and punchline, its type made smaller in steps until the whole card
fits 1200 by 630 pixels. `make og` remakes it (it needs Google Chrome).

`lcc site` builds it from the same scored answers as `make report`: the four models' answers on
the main and stress sets, by every method. It leaves out Gemini 4 Carbon's records, the
stress-candidate selection run and the `lcc check` demo. The export stops if it doesn't hold
exactly the first answers and retries saved on disk, or if it holds a subsection that no quote
lines up with. A quote is lined up with the subsection of its cited section that it matches
best by `quotediff.align`, the alignment behind the quote categories: tokens (words and
punctuation) compared as the quote check compares them, with at least four tokens in a row in
common. The statute text in it is those subsections, each clause's decisive words and the
headings of the sections cited, with the King's Printer notice; the models' quotes and reasons
also repeat the Act's words.

Answers collected 11–13 November 2026 (UTC).

### Headline: a light model with the pipeline vs a heavy model alone

Main test set, 38 clauses. In brackets: 95% bootstrap intervals over clauses (10,000 resamples, fixed seed); for the difference, a paired bootstrap.

| | verdicts right | exact deciding section | cost for the 38 clauses |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Haiku 5.5 + pipeline (light) | 38 of 38 (see Notes) | 30 of 38 (25–34) | $0.036 |
| Claude Opus 5.5 alone (heavy) | 38 of 38 (see Notes) | 33 of 38 (29–37) | $0.77 |
| difference | 0 (see Notes) | −3 (−7 to +1) | |
| Gemini 3.8 Flash + pipeline (light) | 37 of 38 (35–38); 1 unsure | 35 of 38 (31–38) | $0.68 |
| Gemini 4 Argon alone (heavy) | 35 of 38 (31–38) | 32 of 38 (27–36) | $0.072 |
| difference | +2 (0 to +5) | +3 (−2 to +8) | |

A difference counts only if its interval excludes 0; a gap of 1–2 clauses is not called a difference.

Without the contested clauses (c29, c31 and c32; see Notes), 35 clauses, verdicts right and exact sections: Claude Haiku 5.5 + pipeline 35 and 29; Claude Opus 5.5 alone 35 and 32; Gemini 3.8 Flash + pipeline 35 and 33; Gemini 4 Argon alone 35 and 32. The contested clauses are the only ones that Gemini 3.8 Flash + pipeline (c29) and Gemini 4 Argon alone (c29, c31 and c32) got wrong or were unsure on, so those counts are perfect by construction.

### Closed book: the pipeline's question without the statute

Main test set, 38 clauses. The pipeline's question and JSON answer with no statute text in the prompt ([prompts/closedbook-v1.txt](../prompts/closedbook-v1.txt)), asked once, with no retry. Each quote is checked by the pipeline's code against the section it cites, which may be any section of the Act, and the verdict is scored whether or not the quote passes. It shows how well each model recalls the Act's words without the text, and is reported apart from the tables above.

| model | verdicts right | unsure | quote verified | exact section | cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Haiku 5.5 (light) | 21 of 38 (15–27) | 15 | 1 of 23 | 6 of 38 (2–11) | $0.028 |
| Claude Opus 5.5 (heavy) | 38 of 38 (see Notes) | 0 | 25 of 38 | 35 of 38 (31–38) | $0.48 |
| Gemini 3.8 Flash (light) | 38 of 38 (see Notes) | 0 | 19 of 38 | 34 of 38 (30–37) | $0.20 |
| Gemini 4 Argon (heavy) | 36 of 38 (33–38) | 0 | 33 of 38 | 34 of 38 (30–37) | $0.096 |

- **quote verified**: of the answers with a verdict, those whose quote passed the check.
- With the statute in the prompt, 150 of 151 first pipeline answers with a verdict on the main set had a quote that passed.
- A quote that passes the word-for-word check can still stop before the list item that decides the clause. A rough rule in code (`verify.ending`, shown as a warning by `lcc check`, `lcc quote check` and the MCP tools) flags 39 of the 150 passing first pipeline quotes and 21 of the 78 passing closed-book quotes as possibly stopping early. These are upper limits, not counts: the rule flags every passing quote with a list item after it, including quotes that already hold the item that applies. They have not yet been checked by hand.

#### How the quotes that failed the check differ from the Act

Each closed-book quote that failed the strict check against the section it cites, sorted by code ([quotediff.py](../src/lease_clause_checker/quotediff.py)) into the first category that fits. **Drops a negation** (shown only if a quote does): word for word, or but for cosmetic differences, but starting right after a "no", "not", "neither" or "nor" that it leaves out; a narrow check of the one word before the quote, not of a negation's scope. **Passes with quoting conventions**: word for word once an ellipsis, brackets around a cosmetic change, or a changed first capital are read as the marks of a quotation. **Cosmetic**: lines up with the cited section and differs only in articles, punctuation, case, grammatical number (a plural and its verb) or paragraph markers. Number counts as cosmetic because Ontario statutes are read that way: “Words in the singular include the plural and words in the plural include the singular” ([Legislation Act, 2006, s. 67](https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06l21#BK79); e-Laws consolidation from 11 December 2025, read on 14 November 2026; not an official version of the statute, © King's Printer for Ontario, 2006). That is a rule for reading a statute, not for quoting one. **Wrong section cited**: a version of another section, not of the cited one. **Content words differ**: lines up with the cited section, but a content word is changed, added or dropped. **Not in the Act**: lines up with no subsection of the Act. A quote lines up with a subsection when at least half its words match it in order and they make up at least a quarter of the Act's words they span. The categories describe wording, not law: a cosmetic difference is not a wrong statement of the law. Whether a different word changes what the Act says, and if so whether the quote would mislead on the clause being checked, is judged by hand and reported apart from these counts. Every quote, with its difference from the Act, is in [quote-review.md](../results/closedbook-v1+conventions-v1/quote-review.md) (`uv run lcc closedbook quotes`). I worked four rows by hand with Claude to set the approach. Claude then suggested an answer for every row. A first round of blind Claude Opus review, each row judged by one reviewer, surfaced three unclear points, which I settled as written rules; a fourth rule came from rows where the reviewers caught dropped sentence endings. Under the four rules, a second blind round agreed with the suggestions on 46 of 59 rows; on 12 of the other 13 the reviewer's answer was adopted. I approved the result. ([The rules](../results/closedbook-v1+conventions-v1/hand-check/rules.md); [the full record](../results/closedbook-v1+conventions-v1/hand-check/MANIFEST.md).) Not reviewed by a lawyer. Still to come, by Wednesday 18 November 2026: the author's own re-check of 20 rows. It is not fully blind, as the author had seen some of Claude's suggestions. Every category has a reviewed label: Claude drafted, Claude Opus reviewed, the author approved; the hand check agreed with the code's category for 41. Of the 59 quotes, 51 state a rule from the Act, 40 change what it says, and 10 would mislead on the clause being checked (not legal advice; 0 marked unsure).

| model | answers with a verdict | failed the check | passes with quoting conventions | cosmetic | wrong section cited | content words differ | not in the Act | no quote |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Haiku 5.5 | 23 | 22 | 0 | 0 | 2 | 9 | 10 | 1 |
| Claude Opus 5.5 | 38 | 13 | 0 | 4 | 0 | 8 | 1 | 0 |
| Gemini 3.8 Flash | 38 | 19 | 4 | 4 | 0 | 9 | 2 | 0 |

### Failure gallery

Real baseline answers from the main set, quoted from the saved records, then the pipeline's one retry.

**c01, Claude Haiku 5.5, baseline.** Clause: “No dogs, cats, birds or other animals of any kind may be kept in the rental unit or anywhere in the building.” Label: void (s. 14).

> …The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA) does not give tenants a right to keep pets, and it does not address pet ownership.…
>
> …Verdict: enforceable…

Section 14, which the answer cites, says: “A provision in a tenancy agreement prohibiting the presence of animals in or about the residential complex is void.”

**c10, Claude Haiku 5.5, baseline.** Clause: “The Landlord will clean the unit every second Friday and may enter without written notice between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. on those days for that purpose.” Label: allowed (s. 26).

> …A clause that schedules recurring cleaning and permits entry "without written notice" does not fall within any of these exceptions.…

Section 26(2) is that exception: a landlord may enter without written notice to clean if the agreement requires cleaning at regular intervals and the landlord enters at the times it specifies.

**c14, Claude Haiku 5.5, baseline.** Clause: “If the Landlord lists the building for sale, the Landlord may show the unit to prospective buyers. The Landlord will give the Tenant written notice at least 24 hours ahead saying why, on which day, and at what time between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m. it will come.” Label: allowed (s. 27).

> …a landlord may show a rental unit to prospective purchasers only in the circumstances the Act sets out, such as after a notice of termination has been given for a sale.…
>
> …please confirm the exact wording of section 30…

No notice of termination is needed. Section 27(2) lets a landlord enter on 24 hours' written notice “to allow a potential purchaser to view the rental unit”.

**c24, Claude Haiku 5.5, baseline.** Clause: “Rent is payable monthly. Whenever the rent is lawfully increased, the Landlord may require the Tenant to pay an additional amount so that the rent deposit equals the new monthly rent.” Label: allowed (s. 106).

> …the Act does not let the landlord raise the deposit later…

Section 106(3) does: “If the lawful rent increases after a tenant has paid a rent deposit, the landlord may require the tenant to pay an additional amount to increase the rent deposit up to the amount permitted by subsection (2).”

**c14, Claude Haiku 5.5, pipeline: the retry.** The first answer had the right verdict and section, but its quote failed the check (not found):

> A landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry to allow a potential purchaser to view the rental unit.

It is s. 27(2) with “or, with the written authorization of a landlord, a broker or salesperson registered under the Trust in Real Estate Services Act, 2002,” cut from the middle and no mark where the words were dropped. The model was told “The quote does not appear word for word in section 27.” and asked again; the second quote (verified) was the subsection in full:

> A landlord or, with the written authorization of a landlord, a broker or salesperson registered under the Trust in Real Estate Services Act, 2002, may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry to allow a potential purchaser to view the rental unit.

### Notes

- **Perfect scores.** A bootstrap of 38 of 38 only ever redraws right answers, so its interval would be 38–38; the tables say "see Notes" instead. By the exact (Clopper–Pearson) two-sided 95% interval, 38 of 38 is still consistent with an error rate of up to 9.3%.
- **Thinking.** Every model runs at its provider's default thinking setting (for Claude, effort medium). Median billed output tokens per main-set baseline answer, thinking included (Gemini reports its thinking share): Claude Haiku 5.5 1,698; Claude Opus 5.5 872; Gemini 3.8 Flash 888 (thinking 788); Gemini 4 Argon 142 (thinking 0). At its default, Gemini 4 Argon did not think on any main-set baseline answer.
- **Contested labels.** Answers argue against the frozen labels of c29, c31 and c32: a label is listed here when a model's baseline answer argues against it from the Act's own provisions. They are scored as frozen, since the labels were fixed before any model saw the set; the answers are read in full in [verdict-misses.md](../results/baseline-v1+conventions-v1/verdict-misses.md).
  - **c29** (“The Landlord may increase the rent by up to the guideline amount once in any 12-month period, after giving the Tenant at least 90 days' written notice in the form approved by the Landlord and Tenant Board.”) is labelled lawful under s. 116, with s. 119 also accepted. Gemini 4 Argon's baseline answer argued that “once in any 12-month period” could allow an increase less than 12 months after the start of the tenancy, which s. 119 forbids, so s. 4 voids the clause. Wrong verdict in the tables: Gemini 4 Argon (baseline). Also, the clause relies on the guideline that s. 120 sets, but a citation of s. 120 counts as a wrong section. Cited s. 120: Claude Haiku 5.5 (pipeline), Claude Opus 5.5 (baseline), Claude Opus 5.5 (pipeline), Gemini 4 Argon (pipeline).
  - **c31** (“The rent will not be increased during the first 24 months of the tenancy.”) is labelled lawful under s. 119. Gemini 4 Argon's baseline answer argued that a promise of no increase in the first 24 months restricts the landlord's right under s. 119 to raise the rent after 12 months, and the Act can't be contracted out of, so s. 4 voids the clause even though it favours the tenant. Wrong verdict in the tables: Gemini 4 Argon (baseline).
  - **c32** (“Any increase in rent during the tenancy will not exceed the annual rent increase guideline.”) is labelled lawful under s. 120. Gemini 3.8 Flash's and Gemini 4 Argon's baseline answers argued that a promise to keep increases within the guideline conflicts with the Act's routes to an above-guideline increase, such as an application under s. 126, so s. 4 voids it to that extent. Wrong verdict in the tables: Gemini 3.8 Flash (baseline), Gemini 4 Argon (baseline).
- **s17** (stress set: “If the rent is paid after the 5th of the month, a late charge of $50 becomes due.”) is decided by s. 15's “a specific sum becomes due upon a default of the tenant in paying rent due”, independently of O. Reg. 516/06, which as far as we know permits charges for bounced (NSF) payments but not late fees.
- Gemini 4 Carbon was run first and dropped as a top-tier model; records kept.
- Statute words quoted above: Source: Ontario e-Laws. Not an official version of the statute. © King's Printer for Ontario, 2006.

## Statute source and copyright

The statute text comes from [Ontario e-Laws](https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17).
`uv run lcc statute fetch` downloads the current consolidation of the Act in a single request and
saves it, with the source URL and retrieval time, to `.cache/elaws/` (gitignored).
`uv run lcc statute sections 14 15` lists cached sections with their headings, and
`uv run lcc statute check-rules` checks that every rule's heading and link still match the Act.
`uv run lcc clauses review` checks that every test clause cites a rule and quotes its section
word for word (whitespace aside), then writes the review table `data/clauses_review.md`.

What Ontario's [copyright page](https://www.ontario.ca/page/copyright-information) (updated
29 September 2022, read 8 November 2026) says about statutes:

> The King's Printer permits any person to reproduce the text and images contained in the
> statutes, regulations and judicial decisions without seeking permission and without charge. The
> legal materials must be reproduced accurately, and Crown copyright in the legal materials must
> be acknowledged in the following form: © King's Printer for Ontario, 20__.

> Reproductions of statutes and regulations that are not official copies under that Act must state
> that they are not official versions.

The same page says that statutes, regulations and judicial decisions are exempt from the licence
it requires for commercial reproduction of other ontario.ca content.

What this project does as a result:

- The wording of each in-force provision is kept as e-Laws shows it, with only whitespace
  collapsed. The parser leaves out whole paragraphs that are not in-force operative text:
  - citations and amendment histories;
  - subsection headnotes (each section's own headnote is kept as its heading);
  - provisions not yet in force and the notes that introduce them;
  - repealed provisions ("(2) Repealed: …");
  - editorial "Omitted (…)" placeholders (sections 247–263);
  - the table of contents.
- The full statute text is cached locally and **not committed**. The repo contains only section
  numbers, headings, paraphrases and short quotes: in docs, in CLI output, and as each test
  clause's decisive words (`data/clauses.jsonl` and `data/clauses_review.md`). The cache records a
  SHA-256 of the text, so results can name the exact version they used.
- One sentence of another statute is quoted: s. 67 of the Legislation Act, 2006 (S.O. 2006,
  c. 21, Sched. F), in the Results' note on grammatical number, with its own notice and its
  e-Laws consolidation date.
- Wherever statute text is shown, it carries the notice "Not an official version" and
  "© King's Printer for Ontario, 2006". The copyright page asks for "the year of first
  publication of the legal materials"; 2006 is the year in the Act's citation (S.O. 2006, c. 17).

Neither the [terms of use](https://www.ontario.ca/page/terms-use) (updated 27 November 2025, read
8 November 2026) nor the copyright page mentions automated access. The terms say users "must not
… interfere with or disrupt this website", and [robots.txt](https://www.ontario.ca/robots.txt)
does not disallow `/laws/` but sets `Crawl-delay: 1`. The fetcher makes one request and re-uses
the cache after that. It calls the JSON endpoint the e-Laws web app itself uses
(`/laws/api/v2/legislation/...`). That endpoint is not documented, so it may change without
notice.

## Development

Requires [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/).

```sh
uv sync            # install dependencies
make check         # lint, type-check, offline tests (what CI runs)
cp .env.example .env   # only needed for live API runs
```

`.env` is read from the current directory, so run commands from the repo root. The default test
run is offline and free. Tests that call a real API are marked `live` and run only with
`uv run pytest -m live`.

## Related work

Checking a legal quotation against its source is not new, and neither is serving Canadian law
to a language model. Work this project sits beside:

- **Quotation checking.** Thomson Reuters added Quick Check Quotation Analysis to Westlaw Edge
  in April 2020
  ([announcement](https://www.thomsonreuters.com/en/press-releases/2020/april/thomson-reuters-adds-quick-check-quotation-analysis-to-westlaw-edge.html)).
  It compares the quotations in a brief with the US case law they cite and shows the
  differences side by side.
- **Canadian legal text for models.** [A2AJ](https://a2aj.ca/) (Access to Algorithmic Justice)
  serves open Canadian legal data, including through an MCP server, and added Ontario statutes
  in April 2026 ([announcement](https://a2aj.ca/news/2026-04-07-ontario-bc-legislation/)). It
  describes its texts as "unofficial copies collected through automated processes"
  ([data page](https://a2aj.ca/data/)). Third-party MCP servers wrap the CanLII API (for
  example [this one](https://www.vaquill.ai/blog/canlii-mcp-server-canadian-legal-research));
  I haven't found one published by CanLII itself.
- **Grounded citations.** Anthropic's Citations API
  ([announcement](https://www.anthropic.com/news/introducing-citations-api)) has Claude cite
  passages of the documents in its request and return the cited text.
- **Hallucination in legal research tools.** Magesh, Surani, Dahl, Suzgun, Manning and Ho,
  "Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools", *Journal of
  Empirical Legal Studies* 22(2): 216–242 (2025),
  [doi:10.1111/jels.12413](https://doi.org/10.1111/jels.12413), found that commercial
  retrieval-augmented legal research tools still hallucinate, though less often than a
  general-purpose chatbot.

What this project adds to these: statute text taken from Ontario's own e-Laws service, recorded
with its consolidation and retrieval date; an open, deterministic quote check whose code anyone
can read and re-run, with each difference labelled as cosmetic or as a change in content words;
also available as an MCP tool; and an evaluation of how often four
models' quotes of the Residential Tenancies Act pass it, with and without the statute in the
prompt.

## Limitations

- Ontario residential tenancies only, under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.
- The test clauses are synthetic and few (38). They are invented, not drawn from real leases or
  lease templates.
- Each label is meant to be decidable from the clause text and the Act alone, so the test set
  leaves out clauses whose answer depends on outside facts or on regulations, and says nothing
  about how models handle them. Left out:
  - s. 6.1 exemptions, which turn on when the building was first occupied (this is why no clause
    is void under s. 120);
  - key deposits, NSF (bounced-cheque) charges and other amounts that s. 134(1) prohibits
    "unless otherwise prescribed": O. Reg. 516/06 may permit some of them, and it is not in
    this project's corpus.
- Clauses are read as terms of an ordinary private rental: not student housing (s. 37(6)–(7)),
  a care home, a co-operative or a mobile home park.
- The two methods are asked different questions, on purpose. The baseline asks what a tenant
  would type ("Is this clause enforceable?") with no statute text. The pipeline asks whether
  the Act makes the term void, with the relevant sections provided. A label only says whether
  the Act makes the term void, so a baseline answer that calls a term unenforceable for a reason
  outside the Act (the Human Rights Code, say) is scored as a false alarm. Every baseline
  verdict miss is read by hand to check for this: see
  [verdict-misses.md](../results/baseline-v1+conventions-v1/verdict-misses.md). So far none of the
  false alarms came from outside the Act.
- The models' sampling can't be fixed (none accepts a temperature), so a re-run could give
  different answers; the scores are for the saved answers.
- The pipeline is given the same 18 sections for every clause: the sections the test set was
  built on. That is a closed world. A real tool would first have to find the relevant sections,
  and could fail at that step.
- Saved pipeline records replace the statute text in the prompt with a reference (the
  section numbers and the SHA-256 of their text), so the repo doesn't redistribute the Act.
  Re-scoring them needs the same text of those 18 sections in `.cache/`. `lcc statute fetch`
  can only download the current consolidation, so once any of the 18 sections is amended,
  `lcc pipeline report` stops with an error instead of scoring against different text.
  Amendments elsewhere in the Act don't matter.
- The statute text is a dated snapshot from Ontario e-Laws, so later amendments are not reflected.
  Regulations made under the Act are not included.
- The fetcher relies on an undocumented e-Laws endpoint and on e-Laws' HTML classes. The parser
  stops with an error on markup it does not recognise rather than silently dropping text.
- The quote check accepts a quote that starts or ends anywhere inside a subsection. It fails
  a quote that starts right after a "no", "not", "neither" or "nor" that it leaves out
  ("landlord shall, without legal process, seize a tenant's property" against s. 40, whose
  subsection begins "No landlord shall"), but it looks only at that one word: "shall, without
  legal process, seize a tenant's property" still passes. The check shows that the words are
  in the Act, not that they are quoted in full.
- `check_text` pairs quotes and citations by fixed rules
  ([drafts.py](../src/lease_clause_checker/drafts.py)), not by reading the draft. It takes every
  quote beside a citation to be a quote of the Act, so a quoted lease clause in a sentence with
  a citation is checked against that section. It
  reads only double quotation marks (not single quotation marks or indented block quotes),
  reads a range such as "ss. 14-16" as its first section, and tells a statute's title from the
  words before it with a short list of words such as "See" and "Under". A citation with no
  statute named beside it, or with "the Act", is read as a citation of the Residential
  Tenancies Act, even in a sentence about another statute.
- The quote check proves that a quote appears in the cited section. It does not prove that the
  legal reasoning is right, or that the section is the one that decides the clause.
  A quote of five words or more passes even when it stops short of the decisive words, such as
  the opening words of a list without the item that applies.
- The quote categories have known gaps, found in the hand check of the 59 closed-book quotes.
  None is fixed yet; #1 is reported and, for verbatim quotes, #1 and #3 are partly covered by a
  warning (below):
  - Words a quote leaves out before or after the words it matches don't count in its category
    ([#1](https://github.com/present42/lease-clause-checker/issues/1)). Gemini 3.8 Flash's c09 quote of s. 26(1) is sorted as cosmetic although it
    stops before "(a) in cases of emergency; or (b) if the tenant consents". `lcc quote check`
    and the MCP tools name the words of the quote's sentence that it leaves out, where the quote
    lines up with a subsection, as a report only.
  - Openings shared by many provisions can line a quote up with the wrong subsection, or hide
    its source ([#2](https://github.com/present42/lease-clause-checker/issues/2)): Claude Haiku 5.5's c25 quote about a postdated cheque lines up
    with s. 106(4), not s. 108.
  - A fragment that states no rule ("A landlord may enter a rental unit only if") is sorted like
    a full quote, not as too short ([#3](https://github.com/present42/lease-clause-checker/issues/3)).
  - A word hyphenated differently from the Act ("postdated" for "post-dated") counts as a
    changed content word ([#4](https://github.com/present42/lease-clause-checker/issues/4)).
  - A quote spliced from two subsections (Gemini 4 Argon's c17, from s. 37(3) and 37(5)) has no
    flag of its own ([#5](https://github.com/present42/lease-clause-checker/issues/5)).

  Fixing them could move the closed-book category table and the summary's count of quotes that
  differ only cosmetically or by quoting conventions. For verbatim quotes, #1 and #3 are a
  warning beside the strict check (`verify.ending`), not a condition of passing it, so no
  verified-quote count moves. It only looks at where a verbatim quote ends. For a quote that
  lines up with a subsection, the words of its sentence that it leaves out are named, by a
  rough rule for where a sentence ends, but not counted.
  No verdict or section score depends on the categories.
- 38 clauses are few. When two methods both score 38 of 38, the test set can't tell them
  apart, and a perfect score still allows an error rate of several per cent (see Notes under
  Results).
- The stress set was chosen on Claude Haiku 5.5's baseline failures, so its numbers show where
  that model breaks, not how often; it says little about the other models.
